module_title: Sourcing Local Ingredients for African Black Soap

lessons.title: Identifying Key Ingredients: Plantain Skin, Cocoa Pods, Shea Butter, Palm Kernel Oil
lessons.body: To make authentic African black soap, you need four main ingredients: plantain skins, cocoa pods, shea butter, and palm kernel oil. Plantain skins are the black ash that gives the soap its color and deep cleansing power. Use ripe plantain skins (the yellow ones with black spots) because they have more sugar and burn better. Avoid green plantain skinsâthey produce less ash. Cocoa pods are the outer shells of cocoa beans. After farmers harvest cocoa, they often discard the pods. You can collect these pods, dry them, and burn them to ash. The ash adds texture and mild exfoliation. Shea butter is the fat that makes the soap creamy and moisturizing. It comes from the nuts of the shea tree, which grows across West Africa. Unrefined shea butter is bestâit's yellow or ivory and smells slightly nutty. Palm kernel oil is pressed from the seeds of the oil palm. It creates a hard, long-lasting soap with good lather. You can use red palm oil, but it may stain; palm kernel oil is clearer and better for black soap. When you buy these ingredients, look for: plantain skins that are dry and free of mold, cocoa pods that are hard and brown (not soft or green), shea butter that is solid at room temperature and melts in your hand, and palm kernel oil that is clear when liquid and white when solid. A simple test: rub a small piece of shea butter on your skinâit should absorb without leaving a greasy film. For palm kernel oil, smell itâit should have a mild, nutty scent, not a rancid one. In markets, you'll often find these sold separately. A common mix for a 10 kg batch of soap is: 3 kg plantain skin ash, 2 kg cocoa pod ash, 3 kg shea butter, and 2 kg palm kernel oil. Adjust based on your recipe, but these ratios give a balanced soap. Always source from local farmers or markets to keep money in your community and ensure freshness.

lessons.title: Where to Source Ingredients Locally: Markets, Farmers, and Cooperatives
lessons.body: You can find black soap ingredients in three main places: local markets, directly from farmers, and through cooperatives. Each has pros and cons. Local markets are the easiest starting point. In Ghana, go to Makola Market in Accra or Kejetia in Kumasi. In Nigeria, try Onitsha Main Market or Balogun in Lagos. In Kenya, Marikiti Market in Nairobi. Ask for 'plantain skins for soap' or 'cocoa pods for ash.' Vendors often sell them in large sacks. A 50 kg sack of dried plantain skins costs about 30â50 Ghana cedis (roughly $3â5 USD) or 2,000â3,000 Naira in Nigeria. Cocoa pods are cheaperâoften free if you collect from farms, but market vendors may charge 10â20 cedis per sack. Shea butter is sold in balls or blocks. A 1 kg block costs 15â25 cedis in Ghana, or 1,500â2,500 Naira in Nigeria. Palm kernel oil is sold in bottles or jerrycans. A 5-litre jerrycan costs 40â60 cedis. Buying from farmers directly cuts out middlemen. Visit cocoa and plantain farms after harvest season (usually August to November for cocoa, year-round for plantain). Ask if you can buy their discarded skins and pods. Many farmers will sell a pickup truck load for 50â100 cedis. For shea butter, find women's groups in northern Ghana, Burkina Faso, or Mali. They process shea nuts by hand. You can buy 10 kg of unrefined shea butter for 100â150 cedis. Cooperatives are farmer-owned groups that pool resources. In Nigeria, the Cocoa Association of Nigeria connects buyers to cocoa farmers. In Ghana, the Shea Network Ghana helps source shea butter. Joining a cooperative may require a small membership fee (20â50 cedis), but you get consistent quality and fair prices. Always visit in person if possible. Check that the plantain skins are dry and brittle, not damp. Cocoa pods should be hard and dark brown. Shea butter should be smooth, not grainy. Palm kernel oil should be clear when liquid. Build a relationship: buy small amounts first, then increase as trust grows. Pay fairly and on time. This ensures a steady supply.

lessons.title: Sustainable Harvesting and Ethical Sourcing Practices
lessons.body: Sustainable harvesting means taking ingredients without damaging the environment or exploiting workers. For plantain skins, collect only the skins after the fruit is eaten. Never cut down plantain trees just for the skins. Plantain trees produce fruit for several years, so let them live. After you peel plantains for food, save the skins. Dry them in the sun for 2â3 days until they are brittle. This prevents waste. For cocoa pods, work with farmers who already grow cocoa. After they harvest the beans, the pods are discarded. You can collect these pods for free or buy them at a low price. Do not cut down cocoa trees. Instead, support farmers who practice shade-grown cocoa, which protects forests. Shea butter comes from shea trees, which are wild and slow-growing. It takes 15â20 years for a shea tree to produce nuts. Never cut shea trees for firewood or land clearing. Buy from women's cooperatives that harvest nuts by hand, leaving some nuts for the tree to regenerate. In Burkina Faso, the shea industry employs over 100,000 women. Pay them fairlyâa fair price is at least 200 CFA francs (about $0.35 USD) per kg of raw nuts. For palm kernel oil, source from smallholder farms, not large plantations that clear forests. In Ghana, the oil palm industry has caused deforestation. Instead, buy from local women who press oil manually. They use a wooden mortar and pestle, then boil and skim the oil. This method is labor-intensive but sustainable. Ethical sourcing also means no child labor. Visit your suppliers. If you see children working in dangerous conditions, find another supplier. Ask about working hours and wages. A fair wage is enough to feed a family and send children to school. In Nigeria, the minimum wage is 30,000 Naira per month (about $70 USD). Pay at least that for full-time work. Finally, reduce waste. Use every part of the ingredient. Plantain skin ash can be used as fertilizer after soap making. Cocoa pod ash can be mixed into compost. Shea butter residue can be used for cooking or skin care. By following these practices, you protect the land and the people who supply your ingredients.

lessons.title: Quality Checks for Raw Materials: Moisture, Purity, and Contamination
lessons.body: Poor quality ingredients ruin your soap. You must check moisture, purity, and contamination before buying. For plantain skins, moisture is the enemy. Dry skins should snap when you bend them. If they bend without breaking, they have too much moisture. Moisture leads to mold and reduces ash yield. To test, take a handful and squeeze. If they feel damp or leave moisture on your hand, reject them. Purity: plantain skins should be uniform in colorâdark brown to black. If you see green or yellow patches, they are not fully dried. Contamination: look for dirt, sand, or insects. Shake a handful over a white cloth. If sand or dust falls, the skins are dirty. You can rinse them in clean water and re-dry, but it's better to buy clean skins. For cocoa pods, check hardness. A good pod is hard and woody. If it's soft or spongy, it's rotten. Moisture: pods should be dry and lightweight. A wet pod is heavy and will mold. Purity: pods should be whole, not broken into small pieces (broken pieces may contain mold). Contamination: look for white or green mold. If you see mold, discard the pod. For shea butter, moisture: good shea butter is solid at room temperature (below 25Â°C). If it's oily or liquid, it's been heated or mixed with oil. Purity: unrefined shea butter is ivory or yellow, with a nutty smell. If it's white and odorless, it's refined and lacks nutrients. Contamination: look for grit or foreign particles. Melt a small amount in a spoon. If you see dirt, strain it through a cloth. For palm kernel oil, moisture: when liquid, it should be clear, not cloudy. Cloudiness means water or impurities. Purity: it should have a mild nutty smell, not a rancid or chemical smell. Contamination: pour a small amount into a clear glass. Hold it to light. If you see particles, filter it. A simple field test for all ingredients: take a small sample, put it in a clean jar, and seal it. Leave it in the sun for 2 days. If mold grows, the ingredient is too moist. If insects appear, it's contaminated. Always buy from suppliers who allow you to inspect before purchase. If you can't inspect, buy a small sample first and test it. Reject any ingredient that fails these checks.

lessons.title: Negotiating Prices and Building Relationships with Suppliers
lessons.body: Negotiating prices is not about cheating the supplierâit's about finding a fair price that works for both of you. Before you negotiate, know the market price. Visit at least three vendors. In Ghana, a 50 kg sack of plantain skins ranges from 30 to 50 cedis. In Nigeria, it's 2,000 to 3,000 Naira. If a vendor asks for 80 cedis, you know it's too high. Start by asking for a lower price, but be respectful. Say, 'I want to buy regularly. Can you give me a better price?' If you buy in bulk, ask for a discount. For example, if you buy 10 sacks, ask for 10% off. Most vendors will agree if you pay cash. Building relationships is more important than saving a few cedis. A good supplier will save the best ingredients for you. They will tell you when new stock arrives. They may even deliver to your workshop. To build trust: pay on time, every time. If you promise to pay 50 cedis, pay 50 cedis. Don't haggle after the deal is made. Be consistent. Buy the same amount each month. This shows you are reliable. Learn your supplier's name and use it. Ask about their family. In many African cultures, personal relationships matter more than contracts. If you are a woman, you may find it easier to negotiate with women suppliers. In shea butter cooperatives, women often control the trade. Respect their knowledge. They know which nuts are best. Ask them to teach you. When you find a good supplier, stick with them. Don't jump to a new supplier just to save 1 cedi. Loyalty pays off. They may give you credit when you're short on cash. They may warn you about bad harvests. For large orders, consider a written agreement. It can be simple: 'I will buy 20 kg of shea butter per month at 15 cedis per kg for six months.' Both parties sign. This protects you both. If a supplier breaks the agreement, talk to them first. Don't rush to court. In many African communities, elders or market leaders can mediate. Finally, pay a fair price. If you pay too little, the supplier will cut cornersâmix in inferior ingredients or underweight the sacks. A fair price ensures quality and keeps the supply chain healthy. Remember, your business depends on their business.

lessons.title: Storing Ingredients to Prevent Spoilage and Pest Infestation
lessons.body: Proper storage keeps your ingredients dry, clean, and pest-free. Start with a dry, cool room. Humidity should be below 60%. If you live in a humid area, use a dehumidifier or place bowls of charcoal in the roomâcharcoal absorbs moisture. For plantain skins and cocoa pods, store them in burlap sacks. Burlap breathes, which prevents mold. Do not use plastic bagsâthey trap moisture and cause rot. Stack sacks on wooden pallets, not on the floor. This keeps them away from ground moisture and ants. Leave space between sacks for air to circulate. Check every week for mold. If you see mold, remove the affected skins and dry them in the sun for a day. For shea butter, store in a cool, dark place. Heat makes it melt and go rancid. Keep it in a sealed containerâa plastic bucket with a tight lid works. Do not store shea butter near strong-smelling items like onions or kerosene. It absorbs odors. If you buy shea butter in balls, wrap each ball in clean cloth and place in the bucket. For palm kernel oil, store in a glass or plastic container with a tight lid. Keep it away from sunlight. Sunlight makes oil go rancid. A dark cupboard is ideal. If you buy oil in a jerrycan, transfer it to smaller containers to reduce air exposure. Pest control is critical. Rats, mice, and insects love plantain skins and cocoa pods. Set traps. Use cats if you have them. For insects, sprinkle dried neem leaves or ash in the storage room. Neem is a natural insect repellent. You can also use diatomaceous earthâa powder that kills insects by drying them out. Spread it around the base of sacks. For shea butter and palm kernel oil, ants and cockroaches are attracted to the fat. Keep containers sealed. Wipe up spills immediately. If you see weevils in plantain skins, freeze the skins for 48 hours. This kills eggs and larvae. Then dry them again. For long-term storage (more than 3 months), consider vacuum sealing. A vacuum sealer costs about 200â300 cedis, but it prevents spoilage and pests. If you can't afford one, use airtight buckets with gamma lids. Label each container with the date you stored it. Use older stock first. Rotate your inventory. Never store ingredients directly on concrete floorsâmoisture seeps up. Always use pallets or shelves. By following these steps, your ingredients will last 6â12 months without spoiling.

quiz.q: Which plantain skins are best for making black soap?
options: B) Ripe skins with black spots
quiz.explanation: Ripe plantain skins have more sugar and burn better to produce quality ash.

quiz.q: What is the main role of shea butter in African black soap?
options: A) It creates the black color
C) It makes the soap moisturizing
quiz.explanation: Shea butter is a fat that makes the soap creamy and moisturizing.

quiz.q: Which oil is preferred for black soap because it creates a hard, long-lasting bar?
quiz.explanation: Palm kernel oil is pressed from seeds and produces a hard soap with good lather.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for good shea butter?
options: A) It should be liquid at room temperature
B) It should absorb into skin without greasy film
C) It should be pure white and odorless
D) It should smell like chemicals
quiz.explanation: Good shea butter absorbs without leaving a greasy film, indicating quality and purity.

quiz.q: In Ghana, which market is mentioned as a major source for black soap ingredients?
quiz.explanation: Makola Market in Accra is a well-known market for sourcing ingredients.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of buying directly from farmers?
quiz.explanation: Buying directly from farmers eliminates middlemen, often reducing costs and ensuring freshness.

quiz.q: What is a fair price for raw shea nuts in Burkina Faso according to the lesson?
quiz.explanation: A fair price is at least 200 CFA francs per kg to support women harvesters.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid cutting down shea trees?
options: A) They are protected by law
B) They take 15-20 years to produce nuts
quiz.explanation: Shea trees are slow-growing and take many years to mature, so cutting them harms future supply.

quiz.q: What does sustainable harvesting of plantain skins involve?
options: B) Collecting skins after fruit is eaten
quiz.explanation: Collecting skins after the fruit is eaten prevents waste and avoids cutting trees.

quiz.q: Which practice is unethical in sourcing?
quiz.explanation: Child labor is exploitative and should be avoided in ethical sourcing.

quiz.q: What is a sign that plantain skins have too much moisture?
quiz.explanation: Skins that bend without breaking retain moisture, which can lead to mold.

quiz.q: How can you test cocoa pods for contamination?
options: A) Check for white or green mold
B) Smell for a nutty aroma
quiz.explanation: Mold indicates contamination and should be avoided.

quiz.q: What does cloudiness in palm kernel oil indicate?
quiz.explanation: Cloudy oil likely contains water or impurities, reducing quality.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test for moisture in ingredients?
options: A) Seal in a jar and leave in sun for 2 days
quiz.explanation: If mold grows after sun exposure, the ingredient is too moist.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid refined shea butter?
options: B) It lacks nutrients and odor
C) It is harder to store
D) It is not available locally
quiz.explanation: Refined shea butter is processed and loses many beneficial nutrients.

quiz.q: What is a good negotiation strategy when buying ingredients?
options: B) Know market prices and ask for bulk discount
C) Pay after using the ingredients
quiz.explanation: Knowing market prices helps you negotiate fairly and ask for discounts on bulk purchases.

quiz.q: Why is building a relationship with suppliers important?
options: A) To get better prices only
B) To ensure consistent quality and supply
quiz.explanation: Good relationships lead to better quality, priority during shortages, and reliable supply.

quiz.q: What should you do if a supplier breaks an agreement?
options: B) Talk to them first and seek mediation
C) Stop buying from them forever
quiz.explanation: Talking and using community mediation is often more effective than legal action.

quiz.q: What is a fair wage for full-time work in Nigeria according to the lesson?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states the minimum wage is 30,000 Naira per month.

quiz.q: Why is paying a fair price important?
options: A) It ensures quality and healthy supply chain
B) It makes you look good
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Fair prices motivate suppliers to provide good quality and maintain supply.

quiz.q: What is the ideal humidity level for storing black soap ingredients?
quiz.explanation: Humidity below 60% prevents mold and spoilage.

quiz.q: Why should you not store plantain skins in plastic bags?
options: B) Plastic traps moisture and causes rot
quiz.explanation: Plastic bags do not breathe, leading to moisture buildup and mold.

quiz.q: How should shea butter be stored?
options: A) In a cool, dark place in sealed container
quiz.explanation: Cool, dark storage prevents melting and rancidity, and sealed containers prevent odor absorption.

quiz.q: What natural pest repellent can be sprinkled in storage rooms?
options: B) Dried neem leaves or ash
quiz.explanation: Neem leaves and ash are natural insect repellents.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find weevils in plantain skins?
options: B) Freeze for 48 hours then re-dry
quiz.explanation: Freezing kills eggs and larvae; re-drying removes moisture.

quiz.q: Why should you label containers with dates?
options: A) To know when to use older stock first
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps rotate inventory so older ingredients are used first.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of vacuum sealing for long-term storage?
options: A) It prevents spoilage and pests
quiz.explanation: Vacuum sealing removes air, preventing mold and insect infestation.

quiz.q: How often should you check stored plantain skins for mold?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks allow early detection and remediation of mold.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good quality cocoa pods?
quiz.explanation: Hard, woody pods indicate they are dry and free of rot.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid buying shea butter that is white and odorless?
options: A) It is refined and lacks nutrients
D) It is from a different tree
quiz.explanation: Refined shea butter is processed and loses its natural color and scent, along with nutrients.
